goals.title: U0 · Vector arithmetic refresher
goals.description: Use plane and space coordinates, linear combinations and dot products in preparation for linear systems.

goals.title: Start the vector refresher
goals.description: The learner can say which vector operations the refresher will check. Read positions and coordinate changes, then combine vectors and take a dot product. The short check uses both a pair and a triple.

goals.title: Use coordinates and displacement
goals.description:
The learner can represent points and displacements by ordered coordinates in the plane and in space. A point has a position relative to the chosen origin. A displacement records changes in the same coordinate order, so subtract the start coordinates from the end coordinates. For example, from (2, −1, 0) to (3, 1, −2) the change is (1, 2, −2).

In Lecture 1 at 10:42 and 23:12, identify components in the planar and spatial arrows on the board. Then use the coordinate changes in our displacement example.

goals.title: Compute a linear combination
goals.description:
The learner can compute a given linear combination of vectors. Multiply each vector by its scalar, then add component by component. For example, 2(1, 2) + (0, 1) = (2, 5).

At 12:16 in Lecture 1, follow the two scaled columns and their geometric sum. Then compute the different combination given here.

goals.title: Compute a dot product
goals.description:
The learner can compute the dot product of two vectors of the same length. Multiply entries in corresponding positions and add the products to get a number. For example, (2, −1) · (3, 4) = 6 − 4 = 2.

At 4:20 in Lecture 14, check which entries the board example multiplies together. Use just that calculation in this refresher.

goals.title: Check your vector arithmetic
goals.description: Show how you use coordinates, linear combinations and dot products.

examData.taskContent:
1. Starting at the origin of a plane, move 2 units in the negative x direction and 3 units in the positive y direction. Give the point's ordered coordinates. Then give the displacement from (1, −2, 4) to (3, −1, 2).
2. With p = (1, −1, 2) and q = (3, 0, 1), calculate 2p − q. Show the scaled vector and componentwise subtraction.
3. Calculate p · q and show the products you add.

steps.description: Give the ordered pair (−2, 3).
Give the displacement (2, 1, −2) from start to end.
Scale p to (2, −2, 4).
Subtract q componentwise and obtain (−1, −2, 3).
Pair the corresponding entries in the dot product.
Sum the products to 5.

goals.title: Start linear systems
goals.description:
The learner can state the unit plan and the success criterion. Read a system as an intersection and as a weighted sum of columns. Then use elimination and back substitution. In the closing task, explain why three related cases have one solution, infinitely many solutions, or none. MIT lectures write Ax = b. Here we write Au = b because x, y and z already name individual unknowns, so u names the vector that contains them.

At 1:21 in Lecture 1, listen for where the lecturer introduces the two pictures and matrix notation, then name the steps you will use here.

goals.title: Interpret the row picture
goals.description:
The learner can interpret a solution set as the common intersection of lines or planes. A nonzero coefficient row describes a line in two unknowns or a plane in three. A solution lies on every one of these sets. In the figure, x + y = 3 and x + 2y = 5 define two lines that meet at (1, 2). To test a proposed point, substitute its coordinates in each equation.

In Lecture 1, compare the two-line example at 4:20 with the planes drawn from 17:31. In each, identify what the geometric objects have in common.

goals.title: Write a system as Au = b
goals.description:
The learner can encode a linear system as Au = b in a fixed variable order. Put the coefficients of each equation into the corresponding row of A, with a zero for any absent variable. Put the unknowns into u in that same order, and put the right-hand sides into b in equation order. For 2x − z = 4, with u = (x, y, z)ᵀ, the row of A is (2, 0, −1) and the matching entry of b is 4.

At 2:27 in Lecture 1, trace the coefficients of each equation into its matrix row. Look for the order in which the entries are written.

goals.title: Interpret the column picture
goals.description:
The learner can interpret a solution as weights on the columns that sum to b. The coordinates of u weight the columns a₁, a₂, and so on. In the figure, the two-dimensional system has columns (1, 1) and (1, 2), and 1(1, 1) + 2(1, 2) = (3, 5). The column picture is in the space of right-hand sides. The row picture uses the coordinates of the unknowns.

At 8:47 and 22:04 in Lecture 1, trace the weights in the two-column and three-column examples. Find the target vector each sum has to produce.

goals.title: Multiply a matrix by a vector
goals.description:
The learner can compute Av by columns and by row dot products. In the first method, weight each column of A by the corresponding entry of v and add. In the second, take the dot product of each row with v and collect the results in row order. For rows (2, 1) and (0, 3) with v = (1, −1)ᵀ, both methods give (1, −3)ᵀ.

At 36:01 in Lecture 1, follow both ways of computing the same product on the board. Check that they list their result entries in the same order.

goals.title: Eliminate to triangular form
goals.description:
The learner can reduce a square system to triangular form by equivalent row operations, showing pivots, multipliers and row exchanges. Append b to A and apply each operation to the whole row. With pivot aⱼⱼ ≠ 0, subtract (aᵢⱼ/aⱼⱼ) times its row from a lower row to clear that lower entry. The operation can be undone by adding the same multiple back. If the pivot candidate is zero, look below and swap with a row carrying a nonzero entry in the active column. For x + 2y = 4 and 3x + 7y = 13, multiplier 3 leaves y = 1 in the second row.

At 2:34 in Lecture 2, trace the two column-clearing steps on the board. At 11:02, look for the change that makes a row exchange necessary.

goals.title: Solve by back substitution
goals.description:
The learner can solve a nonsingular triangular system by back substitution. Start with the bottom equation, then insert each known variable into the equations above it. For x + y = 5, y − z = 1 and 2z = 6, work upwards to get z = 3, y = 4 and x = 1.

At 17:11 in Lecture 2, follow the board solution from the lowest equation upward. Record which unknown is found at each step.

goals.title: Diagnose singular cases
goals.description:
The learner can distinguish a recoverable zero pivot candidate from a singular system and interpret the outcome in both pictures. Try a row exchange first. If the active column has no pivot, continue with the next column. A square coefficient matrix with too few pivots is singular. A row 0 = k with k ≠ 0 rules out any solution. With no contradiction, a missing pivot leaves a free variable. In x + y = 1 and 2x + 2y = t, t = 2 makes the lines coincide and puts b on the span of the equal columns. If t differs from 2, the lines do not meet and b is outside that span.

Compare the missing-pivot discussion at 11:02 in Lecture 2, the column combinations at 31:06 in Lecture 1, and the zero-row check at 46:02 in Lecture 8. The span means all sums you can make by weighting the columns.

goals.title: Closing task · Linear systems
goals.description: Solve a system using both pictures and elimination, then diagnose two variants. The pass mark is 21 of 25. Equivalent solutions and valid follow-through earn their applicable method points.

examData.taskContent:
1. For x + y = 3 and x + 2y = 5, name the geometric objects in the row picture and find their common intersection.
2. Use the system
   x + y = 3
   2x + 2y + z = 7
   x + 2y + z = 6

   Name its geometric objects in the row picture and give their common intersection when you solve it. Write Au = b in the order x, y, z. Give its columns and explain what their weights must achieve. For v = (2, 1, 0)ᵀ, compute Av both as a column combination and by row dot products. Eliminate to triangular form, including any row exchange, and label the multipliers and pivots. Solve by back substitution, showing the substitutions.
3. Replace only the third equation by x + y + z = s. Can a row exchange restore the y-pivot after first-column elimination? Give the last equation after elimination. For s = 4 and for s = 5, explain how many solutions there are in both the row picture and the column picture. Give the solution family when one exists.
examData.solutionContent:
1. The two equations describe lines. Subtracting the first from the second gives y = 2, so x = 1. The lines meet at (1, 2).

2. The three equations describe planes. The solution below gives their unique common point (1, 2, 1).

   A has rows (1, 1, 0), (2, 2, 1) and (1, 2, 1), with u = (x, y, z)ᵀ and b = (3, 7, 6)ᵀ. The columns are c₁ = (1, 2, 1)ᵀ, c₂ = (1, 2, 2)ᵀ and c₃ = (0, 1, 1)ᵀ. The column equation is xc₁ + yc₂ + zc₃ = b.

   The three row dot products with v give 2 + 1, 4 + 2 and 2 + 2. The column combination is 2c₁ + c₂. Both give Av = (3, 6, 4)ᵀ.

   Subtract 2R₁ from R₂, making R₂ read z = 1. Subtract R₁ from R₃, making R₃ read y + z = 3. The multipliers are 2 and 1. Swap rows 2 and 3 to put a nonzero y-pivot into row 2. The triangular equations are x + y = 3, y + z = 3 and z = 1, with pivots 1, 1, 1. From the bottom, z = 1, y = 3 − z = 2 and x = 3 − y = 1. These are also the weights in the column equation.

3. Apply the same first-column eliminations. Row 2 now reads z = 1 and row 3 reads z = s − 3. Both remaining y entries are zero, so a swap cannot supply that pivot. Use the z-pivot of row 2 and subtract row 2 from row 3 to obtain 0 = s − 4. The square coefficient matrix is singular because it is missing a pivot.

   For s = 4, the first two planes meet along the line x + y = 3, z = 1. The third plane contains that line. There are infinitely many solutions, (t, 3 − t, 1) for real t. In the column picture c₁ = c₂ = (1, 2, 1)ᵀ and c₃ = (0, 1, 1)ᵀ. The right-hand side is 3c₁ + c₃. The total weight 3 can be split between the first two columns in infinitely many ways.

   For s = 5 there is no common point. On the line made by the first two planes, x + y + z remains 4, so the third plane misses the line. In the column picture the first two coordinates of b force the sum 3c₁ + c₃. Its third coordinate is 4, so (3, 7, 5)ᵀ is outside the span.

steps.description: Identify the two lines.
Give their intersection (1, 2).
Identify the three planes.
Give the common point (1, 2, 1).
Give the ordered vector u = (x, y, z)ᵀ.
Give b = (3, 7, 6)ᵀ in equation order.
Give all three coefficient columns correctly.
Identify x, y and z as the respective weights.
State that the weighted column sum must equal b.
Show the dot products of all three rows with v.
Show the column combination 2c₁ + c₂.
Obtain Av = (3, 6, 4)ᵀ.
Use multiplier 2 and obtain z = 1 for row 2.
Use multiplier 1 and obtain y + z = 3 for row 3.
Exchange the two lower rows to obtain the y-pivot and triangular form.
Label the three pivots as 1, 1, 1 in order.
Read z = 1 from the bottom equation.
Use z in the preceding equation to find y = 2.
Use y in the first equation to find x = 1.
Identify both zero y entries, explain why a swap cannot supply the pivot, and obtain 0 = s − 4.
For s = 4, explain the common line and give the solution family.
For s = 5, explain why the three planes have no common point.
For s = 4, give b = 3c₁ + c₃ and explain why equal columns allow many weights.
For s = 5, use the forced column weights to show b is outside the span.
